newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Skanska to give 8-10 bln skr to owners.
newsitem.headline: Skanska to give 8-10 bln skr to owners.

text.p: Swedish construction company Skanska AB said on Tuesday it was looking for a way to transfer eight to ten billion crowns to shareholders and it planned a new dividend policy in the long-term.

Skanska said its 1996 profit after financial items doubled to 5.17 billion crowns ($697.6 million) from 2.57 billion in 1995, boosted by stronger sales and partly by a capital gain of 1.76 billion crowns on shares sold versus 25 million a year earlier.
The company proposed to double its dividend to 10 crowns a share from five, saying it adopted a new dividend policy.

"This policy states that the long-term intention of the group is to pay a dividend equivalent to 3-4 percent of its adjusted equity at the previous financial year-end," Skanska said in its results statement.

The new policy stems from a sharp upturn in consolidated adjusted equity, in turn boosted by a dramatic upturn in the value of real estate and equities as well as by a positive core business' earnings trend.

As Skanska's capital base exceeds the requirements of its core business, the company is "studying the issue of how best to implement additional transfer of 8-10 billion crowns in excess capital back to shareholders," the company said.
Skanska intends to propose suitable measures for such a transfer "in due course."
Skanska's profit after financial items was higher than expected with analysts in a Reuter poll targeting 4.93 billion crowns and a dividend of 5.75 crowns a share.

Its 1996 sales jumped 24 percent to 47.47 billion crowns, of which 46 percent consisted of sales in markets outside Sweden, up from 39 percent in 1995. Order bookings jumped 19 percent to 52.50 billion crowns.
But excluding Skane-Gripen, which was acquired during 1996, sales rose 11 percent and order intake by seven percent, the company said.
Skanska said it had no plans to break up its operations.
The company invested 12.04 billion crowns in real estate, shares and other fixed assets last year with net capital spending reaching 4.54 billion crowns, up from 1.58 billion.

Regarding construction, Skanska said the Swedish market had been weak in 1996 with its operations posting falling order bookings, while its international operations showed a 26 percent increase in order intake to 24.10 billion crowns.
"Operations in the U.S. were the main factor behind the increase, while the total level of order bookings in other international operations was largely unchanged," it said.

Looking at real estate, the book value of Skanska's properties amounted to 21.59 billion crowns, up from 21.48 billion in 1995. Skanska sold 4.38 billion crowns worth of property last year, compared with 2.16 billion a year eaerlier.
The occupancy rate of its property holdings rose to 93.2 percent from 91.7 percent.
